name: Lifestyle lift

lead: The Lifestyle Lift was a branded facelift offered by a national chain of the same name, founded in 2001. It was marketed as a minimally invasive, short-flap procedure done under local anesthesia, with incisions around the temple and ear, tightening of the deeper SMAS layer and removal of excess skin.
Its appearance goal is a firmer jawline and less jowling and neck laxity. A neck-lift technique based on it was described in a 2014 plastic surgery journal article.

paras: Patients booked consultations at the chain's offices and had surgery under local anesthesia with sedation options. Add-ons included chin and neck liposuction, eyelid surgery, brow lifts and fat grafting.

Facelift complications include bruising, scarring, nerve injury and infection, and malpractice studies report litigation in rhytidectomy. The company faced complaints and a 2009 New York settlement over fake endorsements, and it closed in 2015.

chain: Short incisions at the temple and ear
SMAS layer tightened and skin trimmed
angle.text: Surgical tightening is intended to reduce jowls and loose neck skin. The branded version promised a shorter recovery than a full facelift.

lead: The Lifestyle Lift was a branded, minimally invasive 'short-flap' facelift offered by the Lifestyle Lift company, which was founded in 2001 by David Kent, an otolaryngologist and facial plastic surgeon [1]. The procedure used local anesthesia, incisions from the temple hairline around the ear, repositioning of tissue, and tightening of the SMAS layer, sometimes with neck liposuction and muscle sutures [1].

Its appeal was a shorter recovery than a traditional full facelift, advertised through television and infomercials, including spokesperson Debby Boone from 2012 to 2013 [1]. The company grew to more than 50 offices before closing abruptly and filing for bankruptcy in March 2015 [1]. A neck-lift technique called the Lifestyle Lift was described in Clinics in Plastic Surgery in 2014 [2].

The company's marketing drew regulatory attention: in 2009 New York State settled with it over false customer endorsements posted online, with a $300,000 payment [1]. Separately, a 2017 analysis of 89 rhytidectomy malpractice cases found 60 percent resolved in the defendant's favor [3].

paras: The procedure removes excess skin and tightens the deeper SMAS layer through incisions that run from the temple hairline in front of the ear; chin and neck liposuction and neck-muscle suturing may be added [1]. Offices also provided eyelid surgery, brow lifts, laser resurfacing, fat grafting and chin augmentation [1].

Headquartered in Troy, Michigan, the company grew to over 50 offices and more than 100 physicians; its founder was named Ernst & Young's 2012 Entrepreneur of the Year [1]. The company closed its offices in early March 2015 and filed for bankruptcy on March 2, 2015 [1].

Critical coverage in the period included a 2008 television series and reports of a 2009 death in Florida, a 2010 wrongful-death suit and a 2011 lawsuit alleging scarring; the company disputed the accounts [1]. A 2013 Florida Attorney General review found compliance, with no fines [1]. The malpractice analysis found most rhytidectomy plaintiffs were women with median age 56 [3].
A 2014 article describes the Lifestyle Lift neck-lift technique [2]. No randomized trials comparing the branded procedure with other facelifts were found.
